content: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) are the third leading cause of death globally and the leading cause of death in low-income countries. Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), a type of LRTI, is a prevalent condition that imposes a significant health burden, particularly affecting children under five years of age, the elderly, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Antibiotics are the standard treatment for CAP. However, the increasing use of antibiotics has been linked to the development of bacterial resistance and adverse effects in patients. While numerous studies have investigated optimal antibiotic treatments for CAP, most of the available data pertain to hospitalized patients rather than those treated in outpatient settings. This review is an update of a 2009 Cochrane Review and focuses on antibiotic therapies for CAP in outpatient settings. The objective of this review was to compare the efficacy and safety of different antibiotic treatments for CAP in individuals older than 12 years who were treated in outpatient settings. The comparison was based on clinical, radiological, and bacteriological outcomes. To identify relevant studies, the authors searched several databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and LILACS, covering publications up to March 2014. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antibiotics with either a placebo or another antibiotic for the treatment of CAP in outpatient settings. However, no studies comparing antibiotics to placebo were found. Therefore, the review included RCTs that compared one or more antibiotics and reported diagnostic criteria and clinical outcomes. The data collection and analysis process involved independent assessment of study reports by multiple review authors. Any ambiguities in the study reports were clarified by contacting the trial authors. Differences between review authors were resolved through discussion and consensus. This review update included 11 RCTs involving 3352 participants aged 12 years or older with a diagnosis of CAP. Of these, 10 RCTs assessed nine antibiotic pairs (3321 participants), and one RCT evaluated four antibiotics (31 participants). The overall quality of the studies was generally good, although there were variations in the extent of reporting. The studies reported a range of clinical, bacteriological, and adverse events. The findings revealed no significant differences in the efficacy of the various antibiotics studied. However, adverse events varied between antibiotics. For example, nemonoxacin was associated with a higher incidence of gastrointestinal and nervous system side effects compared to levofloxacin. Similarly, cethromycin caused significantly more nervous system side effects, particularly dysgeusia (a distortion of taste), compared to clarithromycin. High-dose amoxicillin (1 g three times daily) was linked to a higher frequency of gastritis and diarrhea compared to clarithromycin, azithromycin, and levofloxacin. The authors concluded that the available evidence from recent RCTs is insufficient to provide new evidence-based recommendations for selecting antibiotics to treat CAP in outpatient settings. The ability to pool data from the studies was limited due to the small number of studies evaluating the same antibiotic pairs. While individual study results did not show significant differences in efficacy between antibiotics, some studies reported more adverse events with cethromycin and nemonoxacin compared to other antibiotics. Further research is needed to compare multiple antibiotics using similar administration schedules to generate robust evidence for clinical practice recommendations. Additionally, future studies should focus on the diagnosis, management, cost-effectiveness, and misuse of antibiotics in CAP and LRTIs across high-, middle-, and low-income countries.
